newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada telecom group to appoint industry ombudsman.
newsitem.headline: Canada telecom group to appoint industry ombudsman.

text.p: The Competitive Telecommunications Alliance, an organization set up by the new entrants to the Canadian long-distance telephone market after it was thrown open in 1992, plans to establish an industry ombudsman to tackle consumer complaints against members.

The office of ombudsman, which is designed to give residential telephone customers recourse to a third party during disputes with carriers in an environment of increasing deregulation by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC), will start operating on November 1.

David McKendry of Price Waterhouse's consumer affairs area will be appointed the first ombudsman. Complaints will be considered by McKendry and the cost of the time taken to deal with them will be billed to the company which is the subject of the customer complaint.

The group has written a lengthy code of ethics which deals with issues like "slamming" -- when a long-distance carrier switches a client to its roster without asking the client's permission first -- as well as acceptable practices for telemarketing, confidentiality of customer records, billing and disputes about charges and termination of a supplier.
The CTA has spent a year consulting with the CRTC, consumer groups and the Bureau of Competition Policy on effective and popular guidelines.

"We thought that if we could take the initiative and set up this thing now, it would serve us well as we head into more and more regulatory forbearance," Donald Braden, executive director of the CTA told reporters.
He said the Stentor group of telephone companies, which includes former monopoly long-distance carrier Bell Canada, will be permitted and encouraged to join the industry group.
Stentor officials were not available for comment.

Braden said all of the CTA's members have opted to join, with the exception of Fundy Cable Ltd and Fonorola . Fonorola has asked for more time to consider the implications of obeying such a code of ethics.

McKendry will rule on complaints that are upheld. If a company fails to comply with a ruling by the ombudsman, that company will lose the right to use the ombudsman group's logo in marketing and advertising. The CTA believes the logo, which has yet to be created, will show consumers that a carrier complies with all the standards of the program.
-- Sarah Edmonds, Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8100, E-mail sarah.edmonds@reuters.com
